solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Alaskan city’s branch or agency downsized (9)

indicatorNotes.downsized: a downsized firm has been cut back, so the phrase loses letters from both ends and what remains is kept

blocks.note: drop BR from the front and NCY from the back; the rest runs across the word break

annotation.surface: A news item about a firm cutting back its office in an Alaskan city.
annotation.walkthrough: The ’s joins definition to wordplay: the city ‘has’ the phrase inside it. ‘Downsized’ reads as corporate cost-cutting, which suits branch and agency perfectly.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this port on Cook Inlet is the most populous city in the state.

entries.clue: Religious leader and a bishop on program (5)

indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, one thing placed on another sits above it, so A and B come before the program

blocks.note: B is the chess notation for bishop
a bot is an automated computer program

annotation.surface: A church leader and a bishop appearing together on a broadcast programme.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Program’ with its American spelling points to software rather than television, which is the nudge towards BOT.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the head of a community of monks leads it in religious life.

entries.clue: Sweet creature eats dairy periodically (7)

indicatorNotes.eats: what an animal eats ends up inside it, so the creature takes the letters in
indicatorNotes.periodically: something done periodically recurs at intervals, so take every other letter

annotation.surface: Some sugary animal nibbling dairy produce every so often.
annotation.walkthrough: The camel opens after its first letter to swallow the pair. ‘Sweet creature’ looks like a term of endearment, but the adjective is the noun definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the noun sense: a chewy sweet, or toffee, made from boiled sugar and butter.

entries.clue: Bananas gone on ripe tree (6,4)

indicatorNotes.Bananas: bananas is slang for crazy, and letters that have gone crazy end up in a new order

annotation.surface: Bananas left on a ripening tree until they go off.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Bananas’ looks like the fruit on the tree, but it is the anagram indicator; only ‘tree’ is definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: it is a regional name for the Douglas fir, a conifer of the American Northwest.

entries.clue: Leader leaves more nuts for summer? (5)

indicatorNotes.Leader leaves: the leader is the first letter, and when it leaves the word loses its head

annotation.surface: A leader departs, leaving a greater stock of nuts for the summer months.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Summer’ is one who sums, not the season; the question mark flags the pun.
annotation.definitionFit: A crossword-only sense: read summer as ‘one who sums’, and a person or device that adds numbers qualifies.

entries.clue: Plant, say, on road plating metal (9)

indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, the first piece sits on top of what follows
indicatorNotes.plating: plating is a metal coating wrapped round something, so the road wraps round the metal

annotation.surface: A plant, for example, beside a road with metal sheeting.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Plating metal’ sounds like electroplating, where the metal is the coating; here the road does the covering.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: it is the sweet briar, a wild rose with scented leaves.

entries.clue: Some soldiers almost laugh involuntarily (5)

indicatorNotes.almost: almost the whole word means stopping one short, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: actors’ slang for breaking into helpless laughter on stage

annotation.surface: A few soldiers who cannot help giggling.
annotation.walkthrough: Theatre slang turns a noun about the dead into a verb about fits of giggles, which is why the surface feels so harmless.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an army corps is a body of soldiers, usually two or more divisions.

entries.clue: It can make parting company bearable at first (4)

indicatorNotes.at first: what comes at first is the opening letter of the word

blocks.note: the .com suffix marks a commercial company

annotation.surface: Something that makes leaving a firm easier to bear.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Parting company’ reads as a phrase about leaving, but the parting is the line in your hair and ‘company’ is split off as wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: drawing a comb through hair is how the dividing line called a parting is made.

entries.clue: Period covered by cost of living? That should get a reaction (7)

indicatorNotes.covered by: something covered by a thing sits under it, so the period goes inside the cost

blocks.note: the payment for somewhere to live
an age is a period of time

annotation.surface: Grumbling about the cost of living, meant to provoke a response.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the pun: the ‘cost of living’ is literally what you pay to live in a place, not the economists’ index.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: chemists add this substance to a mixture precisely to produce a reaction.

entries.clue: Grumpy companion follows friends the wrong way — reckless! (4-5)

indicatorNotes.the wrong way: going the wrong way means travelling backwards, so the word is read in reverse
indicatorNotes.follows: a thing that follows comes after, so the companion goes second

blocks.note: Grumpy and his fellow dwarf in Snow White

annotation.surface: A sulky partner trails along behind friends, heading the wrong direction.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Grumpy’ looks like an adjective, but capitalised it is one of Snow White’s seven dwarfs, and his companion is another dwarf.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word describes a cheerfully careless, devil-may-care attitude.

entries.clue: Animated character with goal to serve drinks (7)

indicatorNotes.with: one thing with another means the two go together side by side

blocks.note: an end is an aim or goal

annotation.surface: A cartoon figure whose aim is to pour drinks.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Goal’ sounds like football but means an aim, as in ‘to what end?’.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the verb comes from the noun for someone who works behind a bar pouring drinks.

entries.clue: Priest protecting poor moves out of Brazil (7)

indicatorNotes.protecting: to protect something is to put yourself round it, so the priest wraps the other word

blocks.note: a lama is a Tibetan Buddhist priest

annotation.surface: A cleric sheltering the poor who are being driven out of Brazil.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Moves out of Brazil’ reads like migration, but the moves are dance steps.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: this fast, close partner dance originated in Brazil and swept the world in 1989.

entries.clue: Largely subdued spy drinks martini finally — it’s shaken not stirred (10)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition is a description: a tambourine is something shaken

indicatorNotes.Largely: largely means for the most part, so keep most of the word and drop its last letter
indicatorNotes.drinks: what someone drinks goes inside them, so the spy takes the letter in
indicatorNotes.finally: what comes finally is at the end, so take the last letter

annotation.surface: A secret agent orders his martini the James Bond way.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Shaken not stirred’ is Bond’s martini order, so Bond is the spy you reach for; the letters need Bourne, and the thing shaken is a percussion instrument.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: this small frame drum with jingles is played by shaking it, and nobody stirs one.

entries.clue: Unenthusiastic response crushes small network (4)

indicatorNotes.crushes: to crush something is to squeeze it, here squeezed tight inside the response

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small

annotation.surface: A lukewarm reaction squashes a small business network.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Network’ suggests computers or contacts; here it is simply a net.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a net of interlaced strands with open spaces is a network in the literal sense.

entries.clue: Abruptly left desk, dazed and confused (10)

indicatorNotes.dazed: something dazed has been knocked senseless, and the letters are knocked out of order

annotation.surface: Someone bolts from their desk in a daze.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Confused’ looks like a second anagram indicator, but it is a plain synonym.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the informal verb means to run off in a hurry.

entries.clue: Plant 41 stops work (5)

indicatorNotes.stops: a stopper plugs a gap, so the number is plugged inside the other word

annotation.surface: A plant closes down factory number 41.
annotation.walkthrough: A 15×15 grid has no 41, so this is not a cross-reference: the number is meant as Roman numerals.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a woodland flower related to the primrose and cowslip.

entries.clue: Sort queen out if one asks for it (2,7)

indicatorNotes.out: sorting something out rearranges it, so the letters go into a new order

annotation.surface: An offer to deal with the monarch’s problem if asked.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Sort’ looks like the anagram indicator, but it is fodder; ‘out’ does the rearranging.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: something available when asked for is offered in this phrase.

entries.clue: Quest — pick outrageous dance (9)

indicatorNotes.outrageous: outrageous behaviour is wild and out of order, as the letters become

annotation.surface: A challenge to choose some shocking dance.
annotation.walkthrough: The Q and K are the giveaway: few dances use both.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a lively ballroom dance in quick time.

entries.clue: Coin toss for fantasy sport (9)

blocks.note: quid is British slang for a pound, and there is a pound coin

annotation.surface: Tossing a coin at the start of a match.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Coin toss’ reads as the ritual before kick-off; here ‘toss’ means throw away.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the airborne ball game played on broomsticks in the Harry Potter books.

entries.clue: Antique unit to get angry about state museum’s leader (5,4)

indicatorNotes.about: about means around, so the anger goes round the other letters
indicatorNotes.leader: the leader goes first, so take the opening letter

blocks.note: to rile is to anger; be riled, get angry

annotation.surface: An antique piece that angers the state museum’s director.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Antique unit’ suggests a piece of old furniture near a museum, but it is a unit of distance.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the ancient measure of a thousand paces, about 1,480 metres, is a unit from antiquity.

entries.clue: Part of US train disturbed calm air (7)

indicatorNotes.disturbed: disturbed things are thrown out of place, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: Turbulence ruffles the still air around an American train.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘US’ flags American usage: the British term would be carriage or van.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use: Americans call a railway carriage a car, and this one carries the post.

entries.clue: English city is a close match? (5)

blocks.note: a city in the East Midlands
a game between teams from the same area

annotation.walkthrough: ‘Close’ means near in place, not tight on the scoreboard: a local derby is played between neighbours.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: an East Midlands city, and a match between local rivals who are close geographically.

entries.clue: Kind of music paper publishing rubbish magazine (7)

blocks.note: a rag is a low-quality newspaper
Time is an American news magazine

annotation.surface: A music paper printing a trashy magazine.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Paper publishing rubbish’ is one long definition of a single word, so don’t look for three pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a syncopated piano style popular around 1900.

entries.clue: Leave South American capital briefly (4)

indicatorNotes.briefly: to put it briefly is to cut it short, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: Quito is the capital of Ecuador

annotation.surface: A quick departure from a South American capital.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Leave’ could be a noun (holiday), but the answer is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to quit a place or job is to leave it.

entries.clue: Artist’s editor wise to pull back (5,5)

indicatorNotes.back: pulling back means going backwards, so the pair of words is read in reverse

annotation.surface: A painter’s editor, shrewd enough to hold back.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Pull back’ looks like a phrase meaning retreat, but ‘back’ reverses both wise and pull together; ‘to’ just runs them on.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the French Impressionist famous for ballet dancers.

entries.clue: Fancy cereal seen regularly in African city (5)

indicatorNotes.regularly: at regular intervals, so take every second letter

blocks.note: the even letters of fancy then cereal

annotation.surface: Posh breakfast food often found in an African city.
annotation.walkthrough: The even letters run across the word break: A, C from fancy and C, R, A from cereal.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the coastal capital of Ghana in West Africa.

entries.clue: In speech, refers to locations (5)

indicatorNotes.In speech: in speech means as spoken, so the word is taken by sound, not spelling

blocks.note: to cite a source is to refer to it

annotation.surface: A speaker mentions some places.
annotation.walkthrough: Both words are said the same; the spelling follows the definition, locations.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: places where something is or happens.

entries.clue: Rising late, nearly curses (4)

indicatorNotes.Rising: in a down clue, rising means going upwards, so the letters are read from bottom to top
indicatorNotes.nearly: nearly the whole word means one letter short, so the last goes

annotation.surface: Someone who oversleeps and nearly swears about it.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Curses’ looks like a plural noun or verb, but read it as the exclamation.
annotation.definitionFit: An interjection for an interjection: both are mild oaths of annoyance.

entries.clue: Save king’s boring quotation? (7)

indicatorNotes.boring: to bore is to drill a hole, so the king drills into the other word

blocks.note: save = except, as in ‘all save one’

annotation.surface: Rescuing a monarch’s tedious remark.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Boring’ reads as dull but means drilling in; ‘Save’ reads as rescue but means except.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, marked with a question mark: a quotation is one kind of extract taken from a text.

entries.clue: It’s played by chamber musician (7)

indicatorNotes.played: letters played with are moved about into a new order
indicatorNotes.by: by means beside, so the two pieces sit next to each other

blocks.note: a cell is a small chamber

annotation.surface: A remark that the piece is performed by a chamber ensemble player.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Chamber musician’ looks like a single phrase, but ‘chamber’ is wordplay and ‘musician’ alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a player of the cello, often found in chamber groups.

entries.clue: Card deck returned to snitch (5)

indicatorNotes.returned: something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters are read backwards

annotation.surface: A pack of cards sent back to an informer.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Returned to’ reads as a phrase about sending back, but ‘to’ is a piece of the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a deck of 78 cards used in fortune-telling.

entries.clue: Man to deal with topping for loaf (9)

blocks.note: to address a problem is to deal with it

annotation.surface: A baker working out what to put on top of a loaf.
annotation.walkthrough: Loaf is rhyming slang: loaf of bread = head. So a topping for the loaf is something worn on the head, not a glaze.
annotation.definitionFit: Rhyming slang: loaf means head, so the ornamental covering worn on it tops the loaf.
